title: A Michelin Chef, a Cancer Survivor, and a 7,500-Sq-Ft Love Letter to Old India: Zamindar's Clubhouse Opens in Charlotte
excerpt: Hyderabad-trained chef Vamshi Krishna Adi brings his Michelin Bib Gourmand pedigree from New York to Charlotte's South End, in a restaurant inspired by the grand clubhouses of colonial-era India.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Zamindar's Clubhouse is a 7,500-sq-ft Indian restaurant in Charlotte's South End.
  • Chef Vamshi Krishna Adi has a Michelin Bib Gourmand pedigree from New York.
  • David Pandoria, a cancer survivor, shifted from corporate sales to restaurant ownership.
  • The menu features diverse Indian dishes, including Hyderabadi biryani and lobster curry.
  • Charlotte's Indian population is growing, increasing demand for high-end Indian dining.
There is a vintage gramophone in the corner of Zamindar's Clubhouse, Charlotte's newest Indian restaurant. Jaipur carpets line the floor. Kolkata-inspired window frames frame the dining room. Khirki-style arches partition a 7,500-square-foot space into distinct rooms — a bar, a lounge, a patio, and a private dining area — each designed to evoke a different facet of India's past. It is, by any measure, one of the most ambitious Indian restaurant openings the American South has seen in years. And behind it stand two men whose paths to hospitality could hardly be more different. ## The Chef: Hyderabad to the Michelin Guide Vamshi Krishna Adi trained at the Culinary Academy of India in Hyderabad before making his way to the United States, where he completed an internship at The Dewberry in Charleston. He went on to cook at some of New York's most respected Indian restaurants — Junoon, which held a Michelin star; Baar Baar; and Rooh in San Francisco. In 2021, he opened Gazab in New York, followed by Ishq in 2024 and KebabIshq in 2025. Ishq was added to the Michelin Guide shortly after opening and later received a Michelin Bib Gourmand designation — the same honour held by restaurants like Khan Saab in California. At Zamindar's, Adi leads a team trained in both India and New York, with a menu that refuses to be pinned to any single region. Jalebi chaat arrives with chickpea masala, beetroot, and crispy sev. Paneer is cooked inside bamboo with coconut and curry leaves. Ghee-roast scallops are dusted with gunpowder alongside crisp koti roti, while pulled venison varuval gets toasted coconut and Malabar parotta. > **""A time when hospitality was an art and dining was a ritual." ## A Menu That Spans the Subcontinent The larger plates draw from cooking traditions across India."** ## The Founder: From Corporate Sales to the Kitchen David Pandoria spent decades in corporate sales, working with Fortune 500 companies. Outside the office, he was a fixture in the Southeast Asian American community as a DJ. In 2023, he was diagnosed with stage-four squamous cell carcinoma. After treatment and recovery, Pandoria decided not to return to corporate life. Instead, he poured his energy into a vision he had carried for years: a restaurant that would recreate the warmth and grandeur of the zamindar-era clubhouses — the social gathering places that once served as the heart of Indian community life, before Partition and independence changed the landscape forever. ![American South — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Andrew_Jackson_monument%2C_New_Orleans%2C_USA.jpg/3840px-Andrew_Jackson_monument%2C_New_Orleans%2C_USA.jpg) "The concept is rooted in the nostalgia of royal households, festive gatherings, and leisurely feasts," the restaurant's description reads. "A time when hospitality was an art and dining was a ritual." ## A Menu That Spans the Subcontinent The larger plates draw from cooking traditions across India. Raw mango and coconut sharpen a lobster curry inspired by Calicut. Sea bass arrives with kasundi cream, poppy seeds, and mustard — a nod to Bengal. The Hyderabadi chicken biryani is Adi's tribute to his hometown.

For dessert, there is a kalakand chocolate tart with basundi, chocolate caviar, and gold dust — the kind of dish that exists somewhere between nostalgia and audacity. The bar programme complements the food with cocktails that draw on Indian ingredients — think cardamom, saffron, and tamarind — alongside a curated wine and spirits selection. ## Charlotte's Desi Moment The timing of Zamindar's opening is no accident. Charlotte's Indian and South Asian population has grown steadily over the past decade, driven by the city's expanding financial services and technology sectors. The metro area is now home to tens of thousands of Indian Americans, many of whom have long commuted to Atlanta or driven to Triangle-area restaurants for a high-end Indian dining experience. The restaurant is located at 155 New Bern Street in Charlotte's South End neighbourhood. Reservations are available through Resy, though the restaurant warns that walk-in guests are seated at the bar only — a sign of the demand it has already generated.
Charlotte's Growing Indian Community
›Tens of thousands of Indian Americans now reside in Charlotte.
›Population growth driven by financial services and technology sectors.
›High demand for elevated Indian dining experiences.
For Indian Americans in the Southeast who have watched New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles dominate the conversation around elevated Indian dining, Zamindar's Clubhouse carries an unmistakable message: the rest of America is catching up. Hours are Tuesday through Thursday 5 PM to 10:30 PM, Friday and Saturday until 11 PM, and Sunday until 10 PM.
